entry:
Indo-Aryan language of [[India]], also known by its endonyms Asamiya and Oxomiya. It is spoken mainly in the northeastern Indian state of [[Assam]], where it is an official language, and it has long served as a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] in parts of [[Northeast India]]. Ethnologue reports over 15 million native speakers and 8.3 million second-language speakers, a claim that academics widely dispute on the basis of census figures. The Government of India designated Assamese a classical language on October 3, 2024, citing its antiquity and literary traditions.

Assamese is closely related to the Kamtapuri language of Rangpur Division in Bangladesh and parts of India, and both descend from the Kamarupi Prakrit. It was in its formative stages in the 12th century CE, evolving from the Magadhi Prakrit. It was the court language of the Ahom kingdom from the 17th century. Nagamese, an Assamese-based Creole language, remains widely used in [[Nagaland]].

Historical action-adventure [[Video game|video game]] series published by Ubisoft. The series, created by Patrice Désilets, Jade Raymond and Corey May, depicts a fictional millennia-old struggle between the [[Order of Assassins]] and the [[Knights Templar]]. The first game was released in 2007. The series has featured 14 main installments, the most recent being *Assassin's Creed Shadows* in 2025. The main games have received generally positive reviews for their visuals, design and narratives, though critics cite the yearly release cycle and frequent bugs. The franchise has sold over 250 million copies as of July 2026, making it Ubisoft's best-selling franchise.

Willful killing, by sudden or secret attack, of a prominent or important person, typically for political, social or ideological reasons.

Assassinations may be ordered by individuals or organizations and carried out by the orderers themselves or by hired accomplices. Assassination is one of the oldest tools of power politics. The Egyptian pharaoh Teti, of the 23rd century BC, is thought to be the earliest known victim. *The Art of War*, a 5th-century BC Chinese military treatise, mentions assassination tactics.

The word *assassin* is believed to derive from *hashshashin*, the name of a group of Nizari Ismailis known as the [[Order of Assassins]], who were active in the Near East from the 11th to the 13th centuries. Notable victims include [[Philip II of Macedon]], father of [[Alexander the Great]], and [[Julius Caesar]]. [[Chanakya]] wrote about assassinations in his political treatise [[Arthashastra]], and his student [[Chandragupta Maurya]], founder of the [[Maurya Empire]], later used them against enemies.

Fatal shooting of the 16th president of the United States at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C., on April 14, 1865. [[John Wilkes Booth]], an actor and Confederate sympathizer, shot [[Abraham Lincoln]] from behind during a performance. Lincoln died the following morning. Booth's conspirators first plotted to kidnap Lincoln, then decided to assassinate him, Secretary of State William H. Seward and Vice President [[Andrew Johnson]]. Only Seward was wounded. Booth was fatally shot in Virginia after a 12-day manhunt. Lincoln was the first U.S. president to be assassinated, and the killing led to a lengthy period of national mourning as the country entered the [[Reconstruction era]].

Shooting in [[Sarajevo]], Bosnia and Herzegovina, on June 28, 1914, of the heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne and his wife.

The victims were [[Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria|Archduke Franz Ferdinand]] and his wife, Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg. [[Gavrilo Princip]], a Bosnian Serb student, shot them at close range as they were driven through the provincial capital. Princip was one of six assassins, coordinated by Danilo Ilić, who aimed to free Bosnia and Herzegovina from Austro-Hungarian rule and establish a common South Slav state. The Black Hand, a Serbian secret nationalist group, helped the assassins. The assassination precipitated the July Crisis, which led to [[Austria-Hungary]] declaring war on Serbia and the start of [[World War I]]. Princip was found guilty of murder and high treason but, being too young to be executed, was sentenced to 20 years in jail.

Fatal shooting of the 35th president of the United States in [[Dallas]], Texas, on November 22, 1963. [[John F. Kennedy]] was shot from the Texas School Book Depository by [[Lee Harvey Oswald]], who was arrested shortly afterward. Oswald was shot dead two days later by Dallas nightclub operator Jack Ruby. The Warren Commission concluded that Oswald acted alone. The 1979 report of the United States House Select Committee on Assassinations concluded that Kennedy was likely “assassinated as a result of a conspiracy”, but its findings rested largely on a police Dictabelt recording that the Justice Department later debunked. Polls show that a vast majority of Americans believe in a conspiracy.

Murder of the Roman dictator by senators in Rome on the Ides of March (March 15), 44 BC. About 60 conspirators, led by Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus, stabbed [[Julius Caesar]] about 23 times during a Senate session. They justified the act as a defense of the [[Roman Republic]], but it failed to restore republican institutions. It precipitated Caesar's posthumous deification and a civil war between his supporters, including [[Mark Antony]], and the conspirators. The conflict ultimately led to the rise of the [[Roman Empire]] under [[Augustus]].

entry: Fatal shooting of the American civil rights activist [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] in [[Memphis, Tennessee]], on April 4, 1968. The escaped convict [[James Earl Ray]] was arrested at London's [[Heathrow Airport]] on June 8, 1968. He pleaded guilty on March 10, 1969, and was sentenced to 99 years in prison, but later made unsuccessful attempts to withdraw the plea. The King family and others believe in a conspiracy involving the U.S. government, the Mafia and Memphis police. In 1999 a civil jury found that Loyd Jowers and others were part of a conspiracy to kill King, but the U.S. Department of Justice disputed the allegations in 2000.

Criminal offense and [[Tort|tort]] involving physical harm or unwanted physical contact with another person, or, in some legal systems, a threat or attempt to cause it.

Assault may result in criminal prosecution, civil liability, or both. Under [[Common law|common law]] systems, assault is distinguished from [[Battery (crime)|battery]]: battery is the actual bodily contact, whereas assault is a credible threat or attempt to cause it. Some jurisdictions combined the two into a single crime called assault and battery, and the civil law and Scots law systems have never distinguished them.

Severity varies. In the [[United States]], assault may be charged as a misdemeanor or a felony. In England and Wales and in Australia it may be charged as common assault, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, or grievous bodily harm. An assault done with intent to kill may be charged as attempted murder.

Select-fire rifle with an intermediate-power cartridge and a detachable magazine. The German *Sturmgewehr* 44 (StG 44) was the first to see major use, during [[World War II]]. The term is generally attributed to [[Adolf Hitler]], who used it as a new name for the MP 43.

By the end of the 20th century, assault rifles had become the standard weapon in most of the world's armies, replacing full-powered rifles and submachine guns in most roles. The two most successful modern designs are the [[AK-47]] and the [[M16 rifle|M16]] and their derivatives.

Low-level programming language closely corresponding to the machine code instructions of a particular computer architecture.

Assembly language usually has one statement per machine code instruction, though it also supports constants, comments, assembler directives, symbolic labels and macros. Each assembly language is specific to an architecture such as [[X86|x86]] or ARM, and an assembler converts it into executable machine code. The first assembly code was described in a 1947 work by Andrew Donald Booth and Kathleen H.V. Britten. In the first decades of computing, systems and application programs were written entirely in assembly. Most programming is now done in higher-level languages, but small amounts of assembly are used within larger systems for performance or to interact directly with hardware. Just under 2% of version 4.9 of the [[Kernel (operating system)|Linux kernel]] source code is written in assembly; more than 97% is in C.

Manufacturing process of progressive, sequential assembly at workstations, in which the unfinished product is moved in a direct line.

Assembly lines are common for complex items such as automobiles, household appliances and electronic goods. Before the [[Industrial Revolution]], most products were made individually by hand. [[Henry Ford]] pioneered the moving assembly line at his Highland Park plant on December 1, 1913, for the [[Ford Model T]], reducing assembly time from over 12 hours to approximately 93 minutes per vehicle. Parts are moved by conveyors, forklifts or gravity, and each worker typically performs one simple operation. The Venetian Arsenal, dating to about 1104, operated in a similar way and at its peak in the early 16th century could reportedly produce nearly one ship each day.

American not-for-profit news agency headquartered in [[New York City]].

Founded in 1846 by five New York City daily newspapers to share the cost of transmitting news of the [[Mexican–American War]], the AP operates as a cooperative whose members are U.S. newspapers and broadcasters. Since the [[Pulitzer Prize]] was established in 1917, the AP has earned 60 of them, including 36 for photography. It distributes the AP Stylebook and election results and sponsors the [[National Football League]]'s annual awards.

Property of certain binary operations, independent of how their operands are grouped.

Within an expression containing two or more occurrences in a row of the same associative operator, the order of the operations does not matter, as long as the sequence of operands is unchanged. Addition and multiplication of real numbers are associative: (2 + 3) + 4 = 2 + (3 + 4) = 9, and 2 × (3 × 4) = (2 × 3) × 4 = 24. Associativity is not the same as [[Commutative property|commutativity]], which concerns whether the order of two operands matters. [[Function composition]] and [[Matrix multiplication]] are associative but generally not commutative. Many operations are non-associative, including [[Subtraction]], [[Exponentiation]] and the vector cross product. In computing, floating-point addition is not associative, and the way an expression is grouped can significantly affect rounding error.

Major ancient civilization of [[Mesopotamia]], dating from the 21st to the 7th century BC.

Assyria was centered in the Assyrian heartland of northern Mesopotamia, and its first capital, Assur, was founded c. 2600 BC. Assyria is called the first true military superpower in human history and pioneered advances in government, bureaucracy, warfare, propaganda and [[Architecture|architecture]]. In the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BC) its army was the strongest in the world, and its empire extended from parts of modern Iran to Egypt, the largest yet assembled. In the late 7th century BC the [[Neo-Assyrian Empire]] fell to a coalition of [[Babylonia|Babylonians]], [[Medes]] and [[Scythians]]. The Assyrian people were among the first to accept [[Christianity]], in the 1st century AD, and the Church of the East developed a distinct East Syriac rite.

Capital city of [[Kazakhstan]], on the Ishim River in the north of the country.

Astana is the second-largest city in Kazakhstan after [[Almaty]], which was the national capital until 1997. Founded as Aqmoly in 1830, the settlement was later renamed Akmolinsk, Tselinograd and Akmola. It was renamed Astana, meaning “capital” in Kazakh, in 1998. It was named Nur-Sultan from 2019 and reverted to Astana in 2022. Kisho Kurokawa guided the decision to turn Astana into a modern and planned city. It has become an important center for culture, education and commerce in Kazakhstan and [[Central Asia]].

Radioactive chemical element with symbol At and atomic number 85, in the [[Halogen|halogen]] group.

Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element in the Earth's crust, appearing only as a decay product of heavier elements, and much less than one gram is present at any time. All of its isotopes are short-lived; the most stable, astatine-210, has a [[Half-life|half-life]] of 8.1 hours. It was first synthesized in 1940 at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and its name comes from the Ancient Greek for “unstable.” Its bulk properties are not known with certainty, but most of its compounds resemble those of [[Iodine|iodine]], and it sometimes displays metallic characteristics. The medically useful astatine-211 is usually produced by bombarding [[Bismuth|bismuth-209]] with [[Alpha particle|alpha particles]].

Large family of flowering plants, also called the aster, daisy, composite or sunflower family.

Most species are herbaceous, though the family includes shrubs, vines and trees, and it occurs on every continent except Antarctica. Its defining feature is the compound flower head, or capitulum, made of many tiny florets enclosed by bracts, which appears to be a single flower. The number of species is rivaled only by the orchid family, Orchidaceae. The oldest known fossils are pollen grains from the Late Cretaceous of Antarctica, dated to c. 76–66 million years ago. The family is economically important, providing food crops such as [[Lettuce]] and sunflowers, garden plants such as [[Dahlia]] and [[Chrysanthemum]], and herbal medicines. Some species become [[Weed|weedy]] or invasive outside their native ranges.

French comic album series about a Gaulish village resisting Roman occupation.

The series is set in [[Gaul]] in 50 BC, when the village's [[Druid|druid]] brews a magic potion that gives superhuman strength. The title character Asterix and his friend Obelix travel to Rome and beyond in many adventures. The series first appeared in the Franco-Belgian comic magazine *Pilote* on October 29, 1959. It was written by René Goscinny and illustrated by Albert Uderzo until Goscinny's death in 1977. Since 2013, Jean-Yves Ferri and Didier Conrad have continued it. As of 2025, 41 volumes had been released, and the volumes have sold 393 million copies, making the series the best-selling European comic book series.

Torus-shaped region of the Solar System between the orbits of [[Mars]] and [[Jupiter]], containing many solid, irregular bodies called asteroids.

The belt is the innermost and smallest circumstellar disc in the Solar System, with a total mass estimated at 3% that of the Moon. [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]], about 950 km in diameter, is the only object in the belt large enough to be classified as a dwarf planet. Vesta, Pallas and Hygiea have mean diameters less than 600 km. Asteroids are grouped by spectra into carbonaceous (C-type), silicate (S-type) and X-type, the last including metal-rich asteroids. The belt formed from planetesimals, but gravitational perturbations from Mars and Jupiter disrupted their accretion into a planet, and 99.9% of the belt's original mass was lost in the first 100 million years of the Solar System's history.

Common long-term inflammatory disease of the airways of the lungs, characterized by recurring symptoms and reduced lung function.

Symptoms include wheezing, coughing, chest tightness and shortness of breath, and they are often worse at night or with exercise. Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors, including [[Air pollution|air pollution]] and allergens. Other potential triggers include medications such as [[Aspirin]] and beta blockers. There is no known cure, but symptoms can be controlled with inhaled corticosteroids, and rapidly worsening symptoms are treated with an inhaled short-acting beta2 agonist such as salbutamol. In 2023, asthma affected an estimated 363 million people worldwide and caused 442,000 deaths, most of them in low- and lower-middle-income countries. It often begins in childhood.

Vision problem in which the lens or cornea of the eye is slightly egg-shaped rather than spherical.

The lack of rotational symmetry causes distorted or blurred vision at any distance and requires lenses with different optical powers at different rotational angles. Treatment options are [[Glasses|eyeglasses]], contact lenses and surgery. Astigmatism is partly genetic in origin. If it occurs in early life and is left untreated, it may result in amblyopia. In Europe and Asia it affects between 30% and 60% of adults. It was first reported by [[Thomas Young (scientist)|Thomas Young]] in 1801.

Argentine tango composer, bandoneon player and arranger.

Born in Mar del Plata to parents of Italian descent, he spent much of his youth in New York City, where he took up the bandoneon. At 17 he moved to [[Buenos Aires]], where he joined Aníbal Troilo's orchestra and studied with Alberto Ginastera. His works revolutionized traditional tango into a style called *nuevo tango*, which incorporated elements of [[Jazz|jazz]] and [[Classical music|classical music]]. He studied composition in Paris with [[Nadia Boulanger]]. His Quinteto Nuevo Tango, formed in 1960, used unconventional instrumentation. Argentine traditionalists derided his work, but it won acclaim abroad. He wrote more than 750 works, including the multimedia opera *María de Buenos Aires* and the piece “Libertango.” American critic Stephen Holden called him “the world’s foremost composer of Tango music.”

Intentional out-of-body experience in esotericism, involving a subtle astral body.

The idea is ancient and occurs in multiple cultures, but the term “astral projection” was coined and promoted by 19th-century Theosophists. It is sometimes associated with dreams and forms of meditation, and some people have reported similar perceptions induced by hallucinogenic or hypnotic means. There is no scientific evidence that consciousness can function separately from normal neural activity or that one can consciously leave the body and observe the physical universe. Astral projection has therefore been characterized as [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]].

Swedish writer of children's fiction and screenplays.

She is best known for children's book series including *Pippi Longstocking*, *Emil of Lönneberga* and *Karlsson-on-the-Roof*, and for fantasy novels such as *Mio, My Son* and *Ronia the Robber's Daughter*. She worked on the [[Children's literature|children's literature]] editorial board of the Rabén & Sjögren publishing house in Stockholm and wrote more than 30 books for children. *Pippi Longstocking* won first prize in a Rabén & Sjögren competition in 1945, after Bonniers had rejected it, and has been translated into at least 100 languages. By 2010 she had sold roughly 167 million books worldwide. In 1994 she received the Right Livelihood Award for her “unique authorship dedicated to the rights of children.” Her campaigning for animal welfare led to a new law, Lex Lindgren, in time for her 80th birthday.
